source: Cognitive Compound Index (basedbiohacker.any.org/cognitive-enhancement, U.S. status as of Oct 2026)
also: Seltorexant, NSI-189, retatrutide, melanotan II, MOTS-c, NAD+, lemborexant, cyproheptadine, selegiline, intranasal insulin, amantadine, memantine, minoxidil, tretinoin, isotretinoin, T3/T4, ginkgo biloba, agmatine, caffeine.

compounds.name: Modafinil
compounds.what: Prescription wakefulness drug approved for narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and shift-work sleep disorder.
compounds.does: Increases wakefulness and alertness, mainly by blocking dopamine reuptake. Used off-label for focus. Rare but serious skin reactions (SJS) are a labeled warning.
compounds.note: Schedule IV controlled substance. Requires a prescription.

compounds.name: Armodafinil
compounds.what: The longer-acting R-enantiomer of modafinil. Same approved uses. It is not an extended-release form of modafinil, as the source says.
compounds.does: Same mechanism as modafinil with a longer duration of effect.
compounds.note: Schedule IV controlled substance. Requires a prescription.

compounds.name: Tadalafil
compounds.what: Prescription drug approved for erectile dysfunction, enlarged prostate (BPH), and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
compounds.does: Relaxes smooth muscle in blood vessels, improving blood flow. Long half-life (about 17.5 hours). Brain blood-flow and performance claims are not established.
compounds.note: Rx only. Dangerous blood-pressure drop if combined with nitrates.

sources.label: GoodRx: prescription prices at U.S. pharmacies

compounds.sourceNote: The source's vendor sells this without a prescription, so it isn't listed. Cheap generics are available with a prescription.

compounds.name: Methylene blue
compounds.what: A synthetic dye approved by FDA as an IV treatment for methemoglobinemia. Oral "USP grade" bottles are sold online outside that approval.
compounds.does: Acts on mitochondrial electron transport. Small studies suggest memory effects; evidence is early. It is a potent MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and many other drugs.
compounds.note: Approved only as an Rx injectable. Oral retail products are unreviewed.

compounds.name: Psilocybin
compounds.what: The psychoactive compound in "magic" mushrooms. Compass Pathways' synthetic version (COMP360) is under FDA rolling review for treatment-resistant depression.
compounds.does: Activates serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Clinical trials show antidepressant effects at supervised doses. Microdosing benefits for focus are not supported by controlled studies.
compounds.note: Federally Schedule I. A few states (e.g. Oregon, Colorado) run supervised programs. No lawful retail sale.
compounds.sourceNote: The source's vendor ships Schedule I psilocybin disguised as an adaptogen blend, so it isn't listed.

compounds.name: Bromantane
compounds.what: A Soviet-developed drug, prescribed in Russia for fatigue (asthenia). Banned in sport by WADA.
compounds.does: Thought to increase dopamine synthesis. Claimed to give stimulation and motivation without a crash. Human data are mostly Russian studies.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. U.S. sellers label it research use only.

compounds.name: Phenylpiracetam
compounds.what: A phenyl-modified piracetam, prescribed in Russia. Banned in sport by WADA.
compounds.does: Stimulant-like racetam. Claimed to raise focus, motivation, and physical endurance. Tolerance builds quickly.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. FDA has warned sellers marketing it as a supplement.

compounds.name: Noopept
compounds.what: A dipeptide drug developed and prescribed in Russia.
compounds.does: Claimed to improve memory and learning and to protect neurons. Mostly animal and small Russian human studies.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. FDA has warned sellers marketing it as a supplement.

compounds.name: Fasoracetam
compounds.what: A racetam once studied in Japan for vascular dementia, then in a small U.S. ADHD trial in children with specific gene variants.
compounds.does: Acts on glutamate (mGluR) and GABA-B receptors. Claimed to give focus plus calm. Human data are limited.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Sold as research use only.

compounds.name: 9-Me-BC
compounds.what: A research chemical from the beta-carboline family. No human trials.
compounds.does: In cell and rodent studies, protects and regrows dopamine neurons; also a mild MAO inhibitor. Long-term safety unknown; it may be light-sensitive and form harmful byproducts.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Sold as research use only.

compounds.name: Bemethyl
compounds.what: A Soviet-era synthetic drug used in Russia to improve work capacity under stress.
compounds.does: Claimed to raise physical and mental endurance and speed recovery. Evidence is mostly Russian literature.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Sold as research use only.

compounds.name: Dihexa
compounds.what: A research compound derived from angiotensin IV, developed at Washington State University.
compounds.does: Boosts HGF/c-Met signaling and new synapse formation in rodents. No human safety data; theoretical cancer-growth concerns because of that pathway.

compounds.name: TAK-653
compounds.what: An investigational AMPA receptor modulator from Takeda, now in trials for depression.
compounds.does: Strengthens glutamate signaling at AMPA receptors. Claimed to speed learning. Only early-phase human data exist.

compounds.name: ISRIB
compounds.what: A lab compound that blocks the integrated stress response in cells, discovered at UCSF.
compounds.does: Restored memory in mouse models of brain injury and aging. No human trials of ISRIB itself.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Sold as research use only.

compounds.name: Mexidol
compounds.what: A Russian drug used for stroke recovery and anxiety.
compounds.does: Antioxidant and membrane-protective. Claimed to improve cerebral circulation and calm anxiety without sedation. Evidence is mostly Russian.

compounds.name: Cerebrolysin
compounds.what: A mixture of peptides derived from pig brain, approved in parts of Europe and Asia for stroke and dementia.
compounds.does: Thought to mimic nerve-growth factors. Trial results in stroke and dementia are mixed.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Injectable with sterility risks from unregulated sources.

compounds.name: Meldonium
compounds.what: A Latvian heart drug for angina. Banned by WADA since 2016.
compounds.does: Shifts cell energy metabolism from fat to glucose. Claimed to aid endurance and focus.

compounds.name: Semax
compounds.what: A synthetic peptide approved in Russia for stroke and cognitive disorders.
compounds.does: May raise BDNF. Claimed to clear brain fog and sharpen attention. Human research is mostly small Russian studies.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. An FDA advisory committee voted in July 2026 to allow compounding; FDA has not finalized it.

compounds.name: Selank
compounds.what: A synthetic peptide approved in Russia for anxiety.
compounds.does: Claimed to reduce anxiety and improve clarity, possibly via GABA and BDNF effects.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Sold as research use only.

compounds.name: BPC-157
compounds.what: A synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide based on a protein in stomach juice. Banned in sport by WADA.
compounds.does: Speeds tendon, gut, and tissue healing in animal studies. FDA found no studies of the routes people actually use in humans.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Removed from FDA's restricted list Apr 2026; panel voted Jul 2026 to allow compounding, pending FDA rulemaking.

compounds.name: Epitalon
compounds.what: A synthetic 4-amino-acid peptide based on a pineal gland extract, developed in Russia.
compounds.does: Claimed to regulate melatonin and sleep and to lengthen telomeres. Evidence is mostly Russian animal and small human studies.
compounds.note: Not FDA-approved. Panel voted Jul 2026 to allow compounding for insomnia, pending FDA rulemaking. Oral capsules are sold as supplements.

compounds.name: Pinealon
compounds.what: A synthetic 3-amino-acid peptide from the Russian bioregulator research program.
compounds.does: Claimed to improve sleep, memory, and stress resilience. Very little published human data.
compounds.note: No FDA status. Oral versions are sold as supplements; injectables as research use only.

compounds.name: Vilon
compounds.what: A 2-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu) from the same Russian research program, linked to the thymus.
compounds.does: Claimed to support immune function and recovery. Evidence is mostly animal.
compounds.note: No FDA status. Sold as a supplement.

compounds.name: Vesugen
compounds.what: A 3-amino-acid peptide from the same Russian program, linked to blood vessels.
compounds.does: Claimed to support blood-vessel health and circulation. Evidence is mostly animal.
compounds.note: No FDA status. Sold as a supplement.

compounds.name: Eutropoflavin
compounds.what: A modified version of 7,8-dihydroxyflavone, a plant-type flavone.
compounds.does: Activates the TrkB receptor, mimicking BDNF in rodent studies. No human trials.
compounds.note: Sold as a supplement; not a recognized dietary ingredient.

compounds.name: NAC
compounds.what: An approved drug (acetaminophen overdose antidote, mucolytic) also sold as a supplement.
compounds.does: Raises glutathione, the body's main antioxidant, and modulates glutamate.
compounds.note: FDA excludes it from the supplement definition but allows sales under enforcement discretion.

compounds.name: Citicoline
compounds.what: A natural compound the body uses to build cell membranes. Prescribed as a drug in Europe and Japan.
compounds.does: Supplies choline for acetylcholine and supports brain cell membranes. Some evidence for attention and memory.

compounds.name: Alpha-GPC
compounds.what: A choline compound found in the brain and in small amounts in food.
compounds.does: Raises choline for acetylcholine production. Some evidence for power output and cognition.

compounds.name: L-tyrosine
compounds.what: A dietary amino acid.
compounds.does: Precursor to dopamine and norepinephrine. Evidence suggests it helps cognition under acute stress or sleep loss.

compounds.name: L-theanine
compounds.what: An amino acid found in tea leaves.
compounds.does: Promotes calm alertness; smooths caffeine's jitters. Reasonable evidence for the caffeine pairing.

compounds.name: Royal jelly
compounds.what: A secretion from worker bees fed to queen bee larvae.
compounds.does: Claimed to support brain health, mood, and testosterone. Human evidence is limited. Can cause severe allergic reactions, especially with asthma or bee allergy.
compounds.note: Lawful dietary supplement. Widely sold by U.S. retailers.

compounds.name: Mastic gum
compounds.what: Resin from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) of Chios, Greece.
compounds.does: Some evidence against H. pylori and for indigestion. Jaw-strength and focus claims are anecdotal.

compounds.name: Magnesium L-threonate
compounds.what: A form of magnesium bound to threonic acid.
compounds.does: Raised brain magnesium in rodents. Small human studies suggest memory and sleep benefits.

compounds.name: Magnesium glycinate
compounds.what: Magnesium bound to glycine; a well-absorbed, gentle form.
compounds.does: Corrects magnesium deficiency; may help sleep and relaxation.

compounds.name: Saffron extract
compounds.what: Extract of the saffron crocus flower.
compounds.does: Several trials show mood benefits comparable to some antidepressants at standardized doses.

compounds.name: Thiamine TTFD
compounds.what: A fat-soluble form of vitamin B1 (thiamine tetrahydrofurfuryl disulfide).
compounds.does: Crosses into the brain better than ordinary B1. Supports energy metabolism and nerve function.

compounds.name: Vitamin E
compounds.what: A fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin.
compounds.does: Protects cell membranes from oxidation. High doses can raise bleeding risk.

compounds.name: Niacinamide
compounds.what: A form of vitamin B3.
compounds.does: Precursor to NAD+, a molecule central to cellular energy and DNA repair.

compounds.name: CoQ10
compounds.what: A compound the body makes for mitochondrial energy production.
compounds.does: Supports cellular energy; often used with statins, which lower CoQ10.

compounds.name: ALCAR
compounds.what: An acetylated form of carnitine.
compounds.does: Moves fatty acids into mitochondria and crosses into the brain. Some evidence in mild cognitive decline.

compounds.name: Vitamin D3 + K2
compounds.what: Vitamin D3 paired with vitamin K2.
compounds.does: Corrects vitamin D deficiency, which is linked to low mood and poorer cognition. K2 helps direct calcium to bone.

compounds.name: Omega-3
compounds.what: Marine fatty acids EPA and DHA.
compounds.does: DHA is a structural brain fat. Evidence supports heart and mood benefits.

compounds.name: Creatine
compounds.what: A compound stored in muscle and brain for quick energy.
compounds.does: Strong evidence for strength and power. Growing evidence for memory, especially under sleep loss.

compounds.name: Zinc
compounds.what: An essential trace mineral.
compounds.does: Needed for immune function, hormone production, and nerve signaling. Long-term high doses deplete copper.

compounds.name: Copper
compounds.what: An essential trace mineral.
compounds.does: Balances long-term zinc intake; needed for energy and iron metabolism.

compounds.name: Vitamin B12
compounds.what: An essential vitamin found in animal foods.
compounds.does: Needed for nerves and red blood cells. Helps cognition mainly in people who are deficient.

compounds.name: Boron
compounds.what: A trace mineral found in fruits, nuts, and vegetables.
compounds.does: Small studies suggest effects on testosterone and bone health.

compounds.name: Selenium
compounds.what: An essential trace mineral.
compounds.does: Needed for thyroid hormone and antioxidant enzymes. Toxic at high intakes.

compounds.name: Taurine
compounds.what: An amino acid abundant in heart, brain, and muscle.
compounds.does: Supports heart function and calms nerve signaling. Recent research links it to healthy aging.

compounds.name: Glycine
compounds.what: The simplest amino acid; a building block of collagen.
compounds.does: Small trials show improved sleep quality. Also an inhibitory neurotransmitter.
